near_miss.why_not: The Norse legal formula names witnesses to a proceeding; Armenian assigns a place-name or describes a person bearing a name. The shared name vocabulary does not preserve the same legal collocation. The closer Norse comparison is within Germanic.

near_miss.lead: Water and fish as a sign of abundance
near_miss.why_not: Irish usce (uisce, subject) and iasc (fish, its yield) occur in a threatened withholding of natural produce, with woods and land. Norse has a fisherman beside water, or water full of fish. Cognate nouns survive, but neither the productive-land curse nor its syntax is shared.
Plautus explicitly refers to giving a true oath. The Irish Fír introduces an assertion about men perceiving the speaker. There is no matched oath construction; a truth word is insufficient.

The assigned Greek historical passages describe military movements, not a death-fall formula. A direct search of both Homer treebanks for falling, earth and death returned Iliad 17.360–363: the earth is wet with blood and bodies fall nearby, but earth is not the complement of falling. This does not establish the same collocation, and the Norse and Greek fall verbs are not cognate.

near_miss.lead: Taunting warriors as daughters rather than men
near_miss.why_not: The Norse speeches shame reluctant fighters as daughters. A recalled Homeric parallel was verified by searching the Iliad text: Il. 2.235 and 7.96 contrast Achaean women and men. The sex-reversal taunt matches, but daughter/father and the Achaean ethnonyms provide no shared cognate phrase. Assigned Greek passages concern a massacre or other matters.

near_miss.lead: Cognate-object or internal-accusative figure: víg er vegit
near_miss.why_not: The Norse expression is an internal-object construction in the passive, concerning a weapon that signals a killing. None of the assigned Greek or Slavic witnesses repeats it or provides a cross-branch cognate construction. A productive internal-object pattern alone is not evidence for this inherited phrase.

The Norse terms identify the same woman through two different relatives. The birchbark text concerns two different women, a sister and her daughter, accused in a dispute. The cognate kin terms do not form the same genealogy or a marked merism.

near_miss.lead: Oath by the deity of the people
near_miss.why_not: The Irish witnesses preserve a recurrent oath: thúath is the people as subject of swearing, with dia as divine referent. The Norse passages have a people settling land, idolatrous kingship, or battle poetry. None supplies the oath construction. Repetition inside Celtic is not a second branch anchor.

Irish hubull is the apple of the hound’s throat in a violent seizure; the Norse apples are literal fruit in Loki’s deception of Iðunn. Greek describes a corpse brought ashore. The throat metaphor is not shared, and the apparent path word in Irish is an OCR split of brágait.

The Norse sentence reports literal snowfall overnight. Umbrian holtu/ninctu belong to a sequence of destructive imperatives in an imprecation. Even accepting the displayed snow etymology for ninctu, there is no common snow-as-subject/fall-as-predicate construction. The etymological proposal is not promoted to a claim.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 956 - PDF page 436 (word id 50768) (w2/3)
near_miss.why_not: The witnesses involve bereavement, ancestry, maternal grandfather, marriage permission, ritual cooking and ordinary parentage. The two inherited kin nouns are basic vocabulary; no distinctive, congruent parental merism or fixed poetic syntax can be isolated across these contexts.

The Norse heart leaps or pounds after an adversary’s identity is revealed. Iliad 22.452 in the slab has a fearful heart throbbing in the chest, but uses ἦτορ rather than the cognate of hjarta; the verbs and chest nouns also differ. An external Homer search found the closer κραδίη ... πατάσσει at Il. 13.282, recorded separately as a search lead. Physiological similarity alone does not establish inheritance.

Irish mairc is plural marc, horses, with lúatha, swift. The Norse mars is a genitive within a skaldic kenning, not a corresponding swift-horse epithet. Sharing the horse noun does not carry the same poetic figure.

near_miss.lead: A sacred lawcourt enclosed with rods and cords
near_miss.why_not: The close Icelandic parallel repeats the same episode and remains within Germanic. Irish rods, royal guarantors and Latin ropes in an agricultural equipment list do not reproduce the court boundary formula across branches.

near_miss.why_not: Norse self-introduction, Armenian third-person genealogy and Old English name-and-people self-identification are broadly comparable narrative acts. The Old English is within Germanic and Armenian does not supply the same distinctive cross-branch construction. Name and daughter words alone cannot establish a phrase.

Irish scarad cuirp ré h-anmain compares a parting to death; Latin Lucretius 3.594 in the supplied context describes soul departing the body. Irish corp is a Latin loan, so the apparently exact body/soul vocabulary is not independent inherited material. The medieval Irish figure can reflect Latin/Christian usage.

Sól and сунце are cognate solar nouns, but the Norse prohibition concerns sunlight on a magic sword, whereas Serbian sets a pre-sunrise time. The predicates differ and ordinary sunlight language does not justify inheritance of a marked phrase.

Irish bláth here concerns the sword’s condition or appearance after custody, within an oath. The Norse stanza explicitly reddens a weapon in men’s blood. The Irish passage does not supply the blood-red collocation and the shared oath witnesses are only Celtic.

near_miss.lead: A fish beaten or pulled ashore
near_miss.why_not: Norse narrates a literal fish hauled home. Irish iasc mbrec, a speckled fish, is the vehicle of a violent simile for Conall’s prospective attack. The beat/pull predicates and the phrase’s function differ; no common inherited collocation is demonstrated.

The Norse weapon fails to bite, but the assigned Russian song speaks of bound and broken limbs, with no weapon-as-biter figure. A direct search in both Homer treebanks for δάκνω with χαλκός or ξίφος found no matching sentence. No cross-branch cognate wording was established.

near_miss.lead: Feeding a raven on enemy corpses
near_miss.why_not: The Irish partners concern battle announcements, spear casting and needle casting, not raven-feeding. A Latin search found Catullus 108.5, recorded separately as an external lead. The cognate corvid noun and comparable hostile death imagery deserve review, but the feeding syntax differs and scavenging is a natural independent motif.

Norse summer and spring occur in a technical explanation of calendar drift. Atharvavedic season lists form parts of a ritual seat or an invocation. Cognate season names are not in the same syntactic or poetic figure; the Norse text is calendrical prose.

Mjúkum orðum describes persuasive speech, but the assigned partners contain place-names, arithmetic or status and lineage. No cross-branch counterpart to the adjective-plus-speech construction is present; no inherited wording is claimed.

search_lead.cognate: Norse hjarta and Greek κραδίη continue the inherited heart noun (*ḱerd-); dattaði and πατάσσει are not cognate.
search_lead.argument: The frightened Norse man’s heart pounds after an adversary is identified; Homer describes the coward’s heart pounding in his chest in anticipation of death. A closer external comparison than the slab’s ἦτορ passage. Treat as a tentative comparison with renewed predicate: ordinary fear physiology remains a strong independent explanation, so no claim is made.

search_lead.cognate: Norse hrafn and Latin coruus are cognate corvid names; svelgja and uorare are different consuming verbs.
search_lead.argument: Norse Hrafn ... ná svelgja is a boast that enemies have been made carrion for a raven (ná, acc. of nár). Catullus wishes an enemy’s extracted eyes to be devoured by a raven. Both express hostile death through the raven’s consumption of the body, with renewed verbs. The Latin eye-detail and curse differ from the Norse corpse-feeding boast; natural scavenger behaviour and the late Norse witness make independent formation plausible. External review lead only.

near_miss.lead: Teeth and biting as weapon imagery
near_miss.why_not: Irish calg ṅ-dét evokes pointed teeth in a noisy army catalogue. Norse has a Thor-image made of tooth material in bundle 40, or a sword failing to bite in 197. The literal tooth object and the biting weapon do not reproduce the Irish collocation; no cross-branch cognate expression was established.

anchors: xcl:MH_1_1_06_Yeghishe ed. page 708 - PDF page 188 (word id 30853) (w1/2)
near_miss.why_not: The Armenian oath invokes deathless gods, while the Hesiodic context has the familiar Greek immortal-gods epithet. This is a possible semantic comparison between two non-pivot witnesses, but the adjective constructions do not establish a distinctive inherited expression here. The Armenian passage is Christian-era representation of pagan speech; the stock divine attribute and possible literary transmission weaken its independence. No secure two-member cognate equation is asserted.
